presentation_slides.title: Unit 1: Acid-Base Equilibria
presentation_slides.content:
Welcome to Unit 1! In this unit, we will explore:
- Three different acid-base concepts
- Ionic equilibria of weak acids and bases
- The common ion effect and buffer solutions
- Salt hydrolysis
- Acid-base indicators and titrations

presentation_slides.title: Learning Objectives - Section 1.1
presentation_slides.content:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:
- Define acids and bases by the Arrhenius concept
- Define acids and bases by the Brønsted-Lowry concept
- Explain conjugate acid-base pairs
- Identify acid-base conjugate pairs from reactions
- Write equations for self-ionization of water and ammonia
- Explain amphiprotic species
- Define acids and bases by the Lewis concept
- Calculate pH from [H+] and vice versa

presentation_slides.title: 1.1.1 Arrhenius Concept of Acids and Bases
presentation_slides.content:
Proposed by Svante Arrhenius.

**Definition:**
- **Acid:** A substance that increases the concentration of H+ ions in aqueous solution
- **Base:** A substance that increases the concentration of OH- ions in aqueous solution

**Strong Acids:** Completely ionize in aqueous solution
- Example: HClO4(aq) + H2O(l) → H3O+(aq) + ClO4-(aq)
- Common strong acids: H2SO4, HI, HBr, HCl, HNO3

**Strong Bases:** Completely ionize in aqueous solution
- Example: NaOH(s) → Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)
- Principal strong bases: Group IA and IIA hydroxides (except Be)

presentation_slides.title: Limitations of Arrhenius Concept
presentation_slides.content:
Despite its success, the Arrhenius theory has limitations:

1. **Limited to aqueous solutions** - Cannot explain acid-base behavior in non-aqueous solvents

2. **Cannot explain bases without OH-** - Ammonia (NH3) is a base but does not contain OH- ions

3. **Cannot explain acidic behavior of some compounds** - Some compounds that act as acids don't produce H+ ions directly

These limitations led to the development of the Brønsted-Lowry concept.

presentation_slides.title: 1.1.2 Brønsted-Lowry Concept of Acids and Bases
presentation_slides.content:
Proposed independently by J.N. Brønsted and T.M. Lowry in 1923.

**Definition:**
- **Acid:** A proton (H+) donor
- **Base:** A proton (H+) acceptor

**Key Advantage:** Not limited to aqueous solutions!

**Example - Ammonia in water:**
NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)

- Water acts as an acid (donates proton to NH3)
- NH3 acts as a base (accepts proton from water)
- NH4+ and OH- are formed - same ions as Arrhenius predicted!

presentation_slides.title: 1.1.2.1 Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
presentation_slides.content:
Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases always occur in **pairs** called **conjugate acid-base pairs**.

**Conjugate Base:** What remains when an acid loses a proton
- HCl → Cl- (Cl- is the conjugate base of HCl)

**Conjugate Acid:** What forms when a base gains a proton
- NH3 → NH4+ (NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3)

**Key Relationship:**
- Species differ by one H+ ion
- Conjugate base has one fewer H and one more negative charge
- Conjugate acid has one more H and one fewer negative charge

presentation_slides.title: Identifying Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1.1:** Identify Brønsted-Lowry acids, bases, and their conjugates.

**Reaction a:**
NH3 + H2PO4- ⇌ NH4+ + HPO42-

- H2PO4- donates a proton → HPO42- (conjugate base)
  - So H2PO4- is the **acid**, HPO42- is its **conjugate base**
- NH3 accepts a proton → NH4+ (conjugate acid)
  - So NH3 is the **base**, NH4+ is its **conjugate acid**

**Reaction b:**
HCl + H2PO4- ⇌ Cl- + H3PO4

- HCl donates a proton → Cl- (conjugate base)
  - So HCl is the **acid**, Cl- is its **conjugate base**
- H2PO4- accepts a proton → H3PO4 (conjugate acid)
  - So H2PO4- is the **base**, H3PO4 is its **conjugate acid**

presentation_slides.title: Strengths of Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Principle:**
- The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base
- The stronger the base, the weaker its conjugate acid

**Example:**
- HCl (strong acid) → Cl- (very weak base)
- CH3COOH (weak acid) → CH3COO- (relatively strong base)

**Direction of Acid-Base Reactions:**
A reaction proceeds in the direction where a stronger acid and stronger base form a weaker acid and weaker base.

**Chart 1.1** (in textbook): Shows the strength relationship between conjugate acid-base pairs in a vertical format.

presentation_slides.title: 1.1.2.2 Autoionization of Substances
presentation_slides.content:
**Autoionization (Self-Ionization):**
A reaction between two identical molecules to produce ions.

**Autoionization of Water (Most Important):**
2H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + OH-(aq)

- One water molecule acts as an **acid** (donates proton)
- Another water molecule acts as a **base** (accepts proton)
- Water is an **amphiprotic** species!

**Autoionization of Ammonia:**
2NH3 ⇌ NH4+ + NH2-

Ammonia can also self-ionize, though to a lesser extent than water.

presentation_slides.title: 1.1.2.3 Amphiprotic Species
presentation_slides.content:
**Amphiprotic Species:** A molecule or ion that can either donate or accept a proton, depending on the other reactant.

**Water (H2O):** The most important amphiprotic species
- With acid: H2O + HCl → H3O+ + Cl- (water acts as base)
- With base: NH3 + H2O → NH4+ + OH- (water acts as acid)

**Other Amphiprotic Species:**
- HCO3- (hydrogen carbonate)
- H2PO4- (dihydrogen phosphate)
- HPO42- (hydrogen phosphate)

**Example:** HCO3- acts as:
- Acid in presence of OH-: HCO3- + OH- → CO32- + H2O
- Base in presence of HF: HCO3- + HF → H2CO3 + F-

presentation_slides.title: 1.1.3 Lewis Concept of Acids and Bases
presentation_slides.content:
Proposed by G.N. Lewis based on electron-pair theory.

**Definition:**
- **Lewis Acid:** Electron-pair acceptor (needs electrons)
- **Lewis Base:** Electron-pair donor (has lone pair electrons)

**Key Advantage:** Most general concept - includes reactions without protons.

**Example - BF3 and NH3:**
- BF3 has only 6 valence electrons → wants 2 more (Lewis acid)
- NH3 has a lone pair of electrons → can donate them (Lewis base)
- Reaction: BF3 + NH3 → BF3-NH3

**Look For:**
1. Empty orbital to accept electron pair (Lewis acid)
2. Lone-pair electrons to donate (Lewis base)

presentation_slides.title: Examples of Lewis Acid-Base Reactions
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1: BH3 + (CH3)2S → H3BS(CH3)2**
- BH3: Boron has only 6 valence electrons → **Lewis acid**
- (CH3)2S: Sulfur has lone pairs → **Lewis base**

**Example 2: CaO + CO2 → CaCO3**
- CO2: Carbon accepts electron pair → **Lewis acid**
- CaO: Oxygen donates electron pair → **Lewis base**

**Example 3: BeCl2 + 2Cl- → BeCl42-**
- BeCl2: Beryllium has only 4 electrons → **Lewis acid**
- Cl-: Chloride has lone pairs → **Lewis base**

presentation_slides.title: Summary: Three Acid-Base Concepts Compared
presentation_slides.content:
| Concept | Acid Definition | Base Definition | Limitation |
|---------|----------------|----------------|------------|
| **Arrhenius** | Increases H+ in water | Increases OH- in water | Aqueous solutions only |
| **Brønsted-Lowry** | Proton donor | Proton acceptor | Requires protons |
| **Lewis** | Electron-pair acceptor | Electron-pair donor | Most general |

**Remember:**
- All Arrhenius acids/bases are Brønsted-Lowry acids/bases
- All Brønsted-Lowry acids/bases are Lewis acids/bases
- The reverse is NOT true!

sections.section_title: Ionic Equilibria of Weak Acids and Bases

presentation_slides.title: Section 1.2: Ionic Equilibria of Weak Acids and Bases
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Describe the ionization of water
- Derive the ion product for water (Kw)
- Explain why water is a weak electrolyte
- Calculate [H3O+] or [OH-] using Kw
- Write expressions for percent ionization
- Calculate percent dissociation of weak acids and bases
- Write and use Ka and Kb expressions
- Calculate pH and pOH from concentrations

presentation_slides.title: 1.2.1 Ionization of Water
presentation_slides.content:
**Autoionization of Water:**
2H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + OH-(aq)

**Key Facts:**
- Water is a very weak electrolyte
- Despite being a non-conductor, it does self-ionize to a small extent
- At 25°C, [H3O+] = [OH-] = 1.0 × 10-7 M

**Equilibrium Constant Expression:**
Kc = [H3O+][OH-] / [H2O]2

**Ion-Product Constant for Water (Kw):**
Kw = [H3O+][OH-] = 1.0 × 10-14 at 25°C

presentation_slides.title: The Ion-Product Constant (Kw)
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Points about Kw:**

1. **Temperature Dependent:**
   - At 25°C: Kw = 1.0 × 10-14
   - At 37°C (body temp): Kw = 2.5 × 10-14

2. **Always Holds:** In ANY aqueous solution at a given temperature
   [H3O+][OH-] = Kw = 1.0 × 10-14

3. **For Pure Water:**
   - [H3O+] = [OH-] = √Kw = 1.0 × 10-7 M

4. **Neutral, Acidic, or Basic:**
   - Neutral: [H3O+] = [OH-]
   - Acidic: [H3O+] > [OH-]
   - Basic: [OH-] > [H3O+]

presentation_slides.title: The pH Scale
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition of pH:**
pH = -log[H3O+] = -log[H+]

**Key Relationships:**
- If [H+] = 2.5 × 10-3 M, pH = -log(2.5 × 10-3) = 2.60
- To find [H+] from pH: [H+] = 10-pH
- If pH = 4.5, [H+] = 10-4.5 = 3.2 × 10-5 M

**pH Classes (at 25°C):**
- Neutral: pH = 7
- Acidic: pH < 7
- Basic: pH > 7

presentation_slides.title: pOH and pH Relationship
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition of pOH:**
pOH = -log[OH-]

**Relationship between pH and pOH:**
From Kw = [H3O+][OH-] = 1.0 × 10-14

Taking -log of both sides:
-log[H3O+] - log[OH-] = -log(1.0 × 10-14)
pH + pOH = 14 (at 25°C)

**Example:**
If pH = 7.40, then:
- pOH = 14 - 7.40 = 6.60
- [H+] = 10-7.40 = 4.0 × 10-8 M
- [OH-] = 10-6.60 = 2.51 × 10-7 M

presentation_slides.title: 1.2.2 Measures of Acid/Base Strength
presentation_slides.content:
There are several ways to measure acid/base strength:

1. **Concentration of H+ and OH- ions**
   - Strong acids → higher [H+]
   - Strong bases → higher [OH-]

2. **pH and pOH Values**
   - Lower pH = stronger acid
   - Higher pH = stronger base

3. **Percent Ionization**
   - % ionization = (ionized amount / initial amount) × 100%
   - Higher % = stronger acid/base

4. **Ka and Kb Values**
   - Higher Ka = stronger acid
   - Higher Kb = stronger base

presentation_slides.title: 1.2.2.3 Percent Ionization
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Percent ionization = (ionized acid concentration at equilibrium / Initial concentration of acid) × 100%

**For Bases:**
Percent ionization = (ionized base concentration at equilibrium / Initial concentration of base) × 100%

**Key Points:**
- Strong acids/bases have nearly 100% ionization
- Weak acids/bases have small percent ionization
- Percent ionization increases with dilution
- For acetic acid at 0.10 M: 1.34% ionization
- For HF at 0.50 M: 3.6% ionization

presentation_slides.title: 1.2.2.4 Acid Ionization Constant (Ka)
presentation_slides.content:
**For a Weak Acid HA:**
HA(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + A-(aq)

**Ka Expression:**
Ka = [H3O+][A-] / [HA]

**Key Relationships:**
- Higher Ka = stronger acid
- Lower Ka = weaker acid

**Example Ka Values (25°C):**
| Acid | Formula | Ka |
|------|---------|-----|
| Hydrofluoric acid | HF | 6.8 × 10-4 |
| Acetic acid | CH3COOH | 1.8 × 10-5 |
| Hypochlorous acid | HOCl | 3.0 × 10-8 |
| Hydrocyanic acid | HCN | 4.9 × 10-10 |

presentation_slides.title: Example: Calculating Ka from pH
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1.5:**
A 0.250 M solution of butyric acid has pH = 2.72. Determine Ka.

**Solution:**
1. Find [H3O+] from pH:
   [H3O+] = 10-2.72 = 1.9 × 10-3 M = x

2. Set up ICE table:
   CH3(CH2)2COOH + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + CH3(CH2)2COO-
   Initial: 0.250 M
   Change: -x
   Equilibrium: 0.250 - x
   [H3O+] = [A-] = x = 1.9 × 10-3 M

3. Calculate Ka:
   Ka = (x)(x) / (0.250 - x)
   Ka = (1.9 × 10-3)2 / (0.250 - 1.9 × 10-3)
   Ka = 1.5 × 10-5

presentation_slides.title: Example: Calculating pH from Ka
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1.5:** Calculate pH of a 0.50 M HF solution (Ka = 6.8 × 10-4).

**Solution:**
1. Set up equation:
   HF + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + F-
   Initial: 0.50 M, Change: -x, Equilibrium: 0.50 - x
   [H3O+] = [F-] = x

2. Use Ka expression:
   Ka = (x)(x) / (0.50 - x) = 6.8 × 10-4

3. Approximation (since Ka is small):
   x2 / 0.50 ≈ 6.8 × 10-4
   x = √(0.50 × 6.8 × 10-4) = 1.8 × 10-2 M

4. Check validity:
   % ionization = (1.8 × 10-2 / 0.50) × 100% = 3.6% < 5% → Valid!

5. pH = -log(1.8 × 10-2) = 1.74

presentation_slides.title: Base Ionization Constant (Kb)
presentation_slides.content:
**For a Weak Base B:**
B(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ BH+(aq) + OH-(aq)

**Kb Expression:**
Kb = [BH+][OH-] / [B]

**Common Kb Values (25°C):**
| Base | Formula | Kb |
|------|---------|-----|
| Ethylamine | C2H5NH2 | 4.7 × 10-4 |
| Methylamine | CH3NH2 | 4.4 × 10-4 |
| Ammonia | NH3 | 1.8 × 10-5 |
| Pyridine | C5H5N | 1.7 × 10-9 |

**Example 1.6:**
Calculate [OH-] of 0.20 M ammonia (Kb = 1.8 × 10-5).

NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-

[OH-] = √(Kb × C) = √(1.8 × 10-5 × 0.20) = 1.9 × 10-3 M

sections.section_title: Common Ion Effect and Buffer Solution

presentation_slides.title: Section 1.3: Common Ion Effect and Buffer Solutions
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Define the common ion effect
- Explain the importance of the common ion effect
- Define buffer solutions
- Give examples of buffer systems
- Explain how buffer solutions resist pH changes
- Calculate pH of buffer solutions

presentation_slides.title: 1.3.1 The Common Ion Effect
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
The common ion effect is the shift in an ionic equilibrium caused by the addition of a solute that provides an ion that is already part of the equilibrium.

**Le Chatelier's Principle:**
Adding a product (or removing a reactant) shifts equilibrium toward reactants.

**Example - Acetic Acid Equilibrium:**
CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq)

When HCl is added:
- HCl provides H3O+ ions (a product in the equilibrium)
- Equilibrium shifts to the LEFT
- Result: Ionization of acetic acid is suppressed

This is the common ion effect!

presentation_slides.title: Common Ion Effect - Another Example
presentation_slides.content:
**Example:** Adding sodium acetate to acetic acid

**Before addition:**
CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO- + H3O+

**After adding CH3COONa:**
CH3COONa(s) → CH3COO-(aq) + Na+(aq)

**Effect:**
- Added CH3COO- is a product in the equilibrium
- Equilibrium shifts to the LEFT
- Less CH3COOH ionizes

**Key Result:** The presence of a common ion from a salt suppresses the ionization of the weak acid/base.

presentation_slides.title: Example: Common Ion Effect Calculation
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1.7:**
Determine [H3O+] and [CH3COO-] in 0.10 M CH3COOH and 0.10 M HCl.

**Given:** HCl is strong acid → [H3O+] = 0.10 M

**ICE Table:**
CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO- + H3O+
Initial: 0.10 M, 0, 0.10 M
Change: -x, +x, +x
Equilibrium: 0.10 - x, x, 0.10 + x

**Ka Expression:**
1.8 × 10-5 = (0.10 + x)(x) / (0.10 - x)

Since Ka is small, x is negligible compared to 0.10:
1.8 × 10-5 = (0.10)(x) / (0.10)
x = [CH3COO-] = 1.8 × 10-5 M
[H3O+] = 0.10 + 1.8 × 10-5 = 0.100018 M

presentation_slides.title: 1.3.2 Buffer Solutions - Introduction
presentation_slides.content:
**What is a Buffer Solution?**
A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, or when diluted.

**Composition of a Buffer:**
- A mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base
  - Example: CH3COOH and CH3COONa
- OR a mixture of a weak base and its conjugate acid
  - Example: NH3 and NH4Cl

**How Does it Work?**
- Contains both acid and base components
- Added acid is neutralized by the base component
- Added base is neutralized by the acid component

**Importance:**
- Biological systems (blood pH = 7.4)
- Chemical processes
- Maintaining optimum pH for reactions

presentation_slides.title: Buffer Action - Example
presentation_slides.content:
**Buffer System:** CH3COOH and CH3COO-

**When Acid (H+) is Added:**
CH3COO-(aq) + H+(aq) → CH3COOH(aq)
- The buffer consumes the added H+
- pH change is minimized

**When Base (OH-) is Added:**
CH3COOH(aq) + OH-(aq) → CH3COO-(aq) + H2O(l)
- The buffer consumes the added OH-
- pH change is minimized

**Net Result:** The buffer maintains a relatively constant pH!

presentation_slides.title: Comparing Buffered vs Unbuffered Solutions
presentation_slides.content:
**Comparison of 1.0 L Samples:**

| Solution | Initial pH | pH after adding 0.010 mol NaOH | pH after adding 0.010 mol HCl |
|----------|------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Unbuffered** (1.28 × 10-5 M HCl) | 4.81 | 2.0 | 2.0 |
| **Buffered** (0.099 M CH3COOH + 0.097 M CH3COONa) | 4.84 | 4.8 | 4.7 |

**Observation:**
- Unbuffered solution pH changes dramatically (4.81 to 2.00)
- Buffered solution pH barely changes (4.84 to 4.7)

This demonstrates the **resisting power** of buffers!

presentation_slides.title: The Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
presentation_slides.content:
**For Acid Buffer:**
pH = pKa + log([conjugate base] / [weak acid])

**Derivation:**
- Start with Ka = [H3O+][A-] / [HA]
- Rearrange: [H3O+] = Ka × [HA] / [A-]
- Take -log: pH = pKa + log([A-] / [HA])

**For Base Buffer:**
pOH = pKb + log([conjugate acid] / [weak base])

**Where:**
pKa = -log Ka, pKb = -log Kb

**Key Assumption:**
The change in concentrations is negligible as the system reaches equilibrium.

presentation_slides.title: Example: Buffer pH Calculation
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1.8:**
What is the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.035 M NH3 and 0.050 M NH4+? (Ka for NH4+ = 5.6 × 10-10)

**Solution:**
1. Reaction: NH4+ ⇌ H+ + NH3
2. Identify components:
   - Acid: NH4+ (0.050 M)
   - Base: NH3 (0.035 M)
3. pKa = -log(5.6 × 10-10) = 9.25
4. Use Henderson-Hasselbalch:
   pH = pKa + log([base] / [acid])
   pH = 9.25 + log(0.035 / 0.050)
   pH = 9.25 + log(0.70)
   pH = 9.25 + (-0.155)
   pH = 9.09

presentation_slides.title: Example: Buffer pH Using Kb
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 1.8 (continued):**
A buffer is made by mixing 0.060 M NH3 with 0.040 M NH4Cl. What is the pH? (Kb = 1.8 × 10-5)

**Solution:**
1. Reaction: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-
2. Identify components:
   - Weak base: NH3 (0.060 M)
   - Conjugate acid: NH4+ (0.040 M)
3. pKb = -log(1.8 × 10-5) = 4.745
4. Use base Henderson-Hasselbalch:
   pOH = pKb + log([conjugate acid] / [weak base])
   pOH = 4.745 + log(0.040 / 0.060)
   pOH = 4.745 + log(0.667)
   pOH = 4.745 + (-0.176)
   pOH = 4.569
5. pH = 14 - pOH = 14 - 4.569 = 9.431

presentation_slides.title: Section 1.4: Hydrolysis of Salts
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Define salt hydrolysis
- Explain why salts of weak acids and strong bases give basic solutions
- Explain why salts of strong acids and weak bases give acidic solutions
- Explain why salts of weak acids and weak bases can give acidic, basic, or neutral solutions

presentation_slides.title: What is Salt Hydrolysis?
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of the cation and/or anion of a salt with water to produce an acidic or basic solution.

**From Greek:**
- Hydro = water
- Lysis = to break or unbind

**General Principle:**
- Ions from a salt can react with water
- One part gets H+, the other gets OH-
- The pH of the resulting solution depends on which ions hydrolyze

**Key Question:**
"What are the parent acid and base of this salt?"

presentation_slides.title: 1.4.1 Salts of Strong Acids and Strong Bases
presentation_slides.content:
**Example:** NaCl from NaOH and HCl

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)

**Net Ionic Equation:**
H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l)

**What Happens in Water?**
- Na+ (conjugate acid of strong base NaOH) → **does NOT hydrolyze**
- Cl- (conjugate base of strong acid HCl) → **does NOT hydrolyze**

**Result:**
- No ion reacts with water
- Solution is **neutral** (pH = 7)

**Other Examples:**
KCl, NaNO3, KNO3, CaCl2, KBr

presentation_slides.title: 1.4.2 Salts of Weak Acids and Strong Bases
presentation_slides.content:
**Example:** CH3COONa from CH3COOH and NaOH

CH3COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) → CH3COONa(aq) + H2O(l)

**What Happens in Water?**
- Na+ → **does NOT hydrolyze** (from strong base)
- CH3COO- (conjugate base of weak acid) → **DOES hydrolyze**

**Hydrolysis Reaction:**
CH3COO-(aq) + H2O(aq) ⇌ CH3COOH(aq) + OH-(aq)

**Result:**
- OH- ions are produced
- Solution is **basic** (pH > 7)

**General Rule:**
Salts of weak acids and strong bases give **basic** solutions.

presentation_slides.title: 1.4.3 Salts of Strong Acids and Weak Bases
presentation_slides.content:
**Example:** NH4Cl from NH3 and HCl

NH3(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH4Cl(aq)

**What Happens in Water?**
- Cl- → **does NOT hydrolyze** (from strong acid)
- NH4+ (conjugate acid of weak base) → **DOES hydrolyze**

**Hydrolysis Reaction:**
NH4+(aq) + H2O(aq) ⇌ NH3(aq) + H3O+(aq)

**Result:**
- H3O+ ions are produced
- Solution is **acidic** (pH < 7)

**General Rule:**
Salts of strong acids and weak bases give **acidic** solutions.

presentation_slides.title: 1.4.4 Salts of Weak Acids and Weak Bases
presentation_slides.content:
**Example:** NH4F from NH3 and HF

**Both ions can hydrolyze:**
- NH4+ (conjugate acid of weak base NH3) produces H3O+
  NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O+
- F- (conjugate base of weak acid HF) produces OH-
  F- + H2O ⇌ HF + OH-

**Determining the pH:**
- Compare Ka of the cation (NH4+ = 5.6 × 10-10)
- Compare Kb of the anion (F- = 1.4 × 10-11)

**Rule:**
- If Ka > Kb → acidic solution
- If Kb > Ka → basic solution
- If Ka = Kb → neutral solution

presentation_slides.title: Example: Predicting Salt Solution pH
presentation_slides.content:
**Problem:** Determine whether solutions of NH4F, NH4CNS, and CH3COONH4 are acidic, basic, or neutral.

**Given Values:**
| Anion | Kb | Cation | Ka |
|-------|-----|--------|-----|
| F- | 1.4 × 10-11 | NH4+ | 5.6 × 10-10 |
| CNS- | 2.0 × 10-5 | NH4+ | 5.6 × 10-10 |
| CH3COO- | 5.6 × 10-10 | NH4+ | 5.6 × 10-10 |

**Analysis:**
- **NH4F:** Ka(5.6 × 10-10) > Kb(1.4 × 10-11) → **Acidic**
- **NH4CNS:** Kb(2.0 × 10-5) > Ka(5.6 × 10-10) → **Basic**
- **CH3COONH4:** Ka(5.6 × 10-10) = Kb(5.6 × 10-10) → **Neutral**

presentation_slides.title: Section 1.5: Acid-Base Indicators and Titrations
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Define acid-base indicators and give examples
- Suggest suitable indicators for acid-base titrations
- Explain equivalents of acids and bases
- Calculate normality of acidic/basic solutions
- Define acid-base titration
- Distinguish between end point and equivalence point
- Discuss titration curves

presentation_slides.title: 1.5.1 Acid-Base Indicators
presentation_slides.content:
**What are Acid-Base Indicators?**
Weak organic acids (HIn) or bases (In-) that indicate whether a solution is acidic, basic, or neutral.

**How They Work:**
HIn + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + In-
(Acid color) (Base color)

**Le Chatelier's Principle:**
- In acidic medium (high [H3O+]): Equilibrium shifts LEFT → Acid color
- In basic medium (low [H3O+]): Equilibrium shifts RIGHT → Base color

**Key Point:**
A small amount of indicator does NOT affect the pH of the solution.

presentation_slides.title: Common Acid-Base Indicators
presentation_slides.content:
**Common Indicators and Their pH Ranges:**

| Indicator | Acid Color | Base Color | pH Range |
|-----------|------------|------------|----------|
| Methyl violet | Yellow | Violet | 0.0 - 1.6 |
| Methyl orange | Red | Yellow | 3.2 - 4.4 |
| Bromcresol green | Yellow | Blue | 3.8 - 5.4 |
| Methyl red | Red | Yellow | 4.8 - 6.0 |
| Litmus | Red | Blue | 5.0 - 8.0 |
| Phenolphthalein | Colorless | Pink | 8.2 - 10.0 |

**Example:**
For a buffer with pH = 4.44, methyl orange (3.2-4.4) would show yellow color.

presentation_slides.title: 1.5.2 Equivalents of Acids and Bases
presentation_slides.content:
**What is an Equivalent?**
The amount of a substance that reacts with or supplies one mole of H+ ions in an acid-base reaction.

**For Acids:**
- HCl: 1 equivalent (provides 1 H+)
- H2SO4: 2 equivalents (provides 2 H+)
- H3PO4: 3 equivalents (provides 3 H+)

**For Bases:**
- NaOH: 1 equivalent (provides 1 OH-)
- Ca(OH)2: 2 equivalents (provides 2 OH-)
- Al(OH)3: 3 equivalents (provides 3 OH-)

**Normality (N):**
Normality = Number of equivalents of solute / Liters of solution

presentation_slides.title: Normality in Acid-Base Reactions
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Equation for Titration:**
N1 × V1 = N2 × V2 (for acid-base neutralization)

Where:
- N1 = Normality of acid
- V1 = Volume of acid
- N2 = Normality of base
- V2 = Volume of base

**Example 1.10:**
What volume of 2.0 N NaOH is required to neutralize 25.0 mL of 2.70 N H2SO4?

**Solution:**
V2 = (N1 × V1) / N2
V2 = (2.70 N × 25.0 mL) / 2.0 N
V2 = 33.8 mL NaOH

presentation_slides.title: 1.5.3 Acid-Base Titrations - Introduction
presentation_slides.content:
**What is an Acid-Base Titration?**
A procedure for determining the amount of acid (or base) in a solution by determining the volume of base (or acid) of known concentration that will completely react with it.

**Key Terms:**
- **Titrant:** The solution of known concentration added from the burette (usually the base)
- **Analyte:** The solution of unknown concentration being analyzed (usually the acid)
- **Equivalence Point:** The point at which moles of acid = moles of base
- **End Point:** The point at which the indicator changes color
- **Titration Curve:** A plot of pH vs. volume of titrant added

presentation_slides.title: Equivalence Point vs. End Point
presentation_slides.content:
**Equivalence Point:**
- Stoichiometric point
- Moles of acid = Moles of base
- Theoretical point based on calculations
- Solution contains only salt and water

**End Point:**
- Observational point
- Where indicator changes color
- Should match the equivalence point

**Ideal Titration:**
The end point should be as close as possible to the equivalence point.

**Indicator Selection:**
Choose an indicator whose pH range includes the pH of the equivalence point.

presentation_slides.title: Titration Experiment
presentation_slides.content:
**Experiment 1.1: Acid-Base Titration**

**Objective:** Find the normality of a given HCl solution by titrating against 0.1 N NaOH.

**Apparatus:**
- 10 mL pipette, burette, 150 mL Erlenmeyer flask, beaker, funnel

**Procedure Summary:**
1. Clean and rinse burette with NaOH solution
2. Fill burette with 0.1 N NaOH (record initial volume)
3. Measure exactly 10 mL of HCl into flask
4. Add 2-3 drops of phenolphthalein indicator
5. Titrate until pink color persists
6. Record final volume

**Calculations:**
V(NaOH) × N(NaOH) = V(HCl) × N(HCl)

presentation_slides.title: Unit 2: Electrochemistry
presentation_slides.content:
Welcome to Unit 2! In this unit, we will explore:
- Oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions
- Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
- Quantitative aspects of electrolysis
- Industrial applications of electrolysis
- Voltaic cells
- Corrosion and its prevention

presentation_slides.title: Section 2.1: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
presentation_slides.content:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:
- Define redox reactions
- Define oxidation in terms of electron transfer and change in oxidation number
- Define reduction in terms of electron transfer and change in oxidation number
- Identify oxidizing and reducing agents
- Balance redox reactions using oxidation number and half-reaction methods

presentation_slides.title: 2.1.1 Oxidation - Definition
presentation_slides.content:
**Original Definition:**
The addition of oxygen to a compound.

**Modern Definition:**
Oxidation is a process in which an atom/element:
- **Loses electrons**
- **Increases its oxidation number**

**Examples:**
- Mg → Mg2+ + 2e- (loses 2 electrons)
- Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e- (loses 1 electron)
- S2- → S + 2e- (loses 2 electrons)

**Key Concept:**
The species that is oxidized is called the **reducing agent**.

presentation_slides.title: 2.1.2 Reduction - Definition
presentation_slides.content:
**Original Definition:**
The production of a metal from its ore (removal of oxygen).

**Modern Definition:**
Reduction is a process in which an atom/element:
- **Gains electrons**
- **Decreases its oxidation number**

**Examples:**
- Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (gains 2 electrons)
- Fe3+ + e- → Fe2+ (gains 1 electron)
- Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl- (gains 2 electrons)

**Key Concept:**
The species that is reduced is called the **oxidizing agent**.

presentation_slides.title: Redox Reactions - Key Concepts
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
A redox reaction involves the transfer of electrons from a reducing agent to an oxidizing agent.

**Key Points:**
1. Oxidation and reduction ALWAYS occur together
2. Can't have one without the other!
3. The number of electrons lost = number of electrons gained

**Example:**
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

- Mg: 0 → +2 (losses 2e-) → **Oxidized**
- H+: +1 → 0 (gains 2e-) → **Reduced**
- Cl-: spectator ions

**Reducing Agent:** Mg (causes reduction of H+)
**Oxidizing Agent:** H+ (causes oxidation of Mg)

presentation_slides.title: 2.1.3 Balancing Redox Reactions
presentation_slides.content:
**Two Methods for Balancing Redox Reactions:**

**1. Change in Oxidation Number Method:**
- Used for reactions not in aqueous solution
- Uses changes in oxidation numbers to balance electrons

**2. Half-Reaction Method (Ion-Electron Method):**
- Used for reactions in aqueous solution
- Separates into oxidation and reduction half-reactions
- Balances atoms and charges separately

presentation_slides.title: Oxidation Number Method - Steps
presentation_slides.content:
**Step 1:** Write the unbalanced chemical equation

**Step 2:** Assign oxidation numbers to all elements

**Step 3:** Identify oxidized and reduced species

**Step 4:** Compute electrons lost and gained

**Step 5:** Multiply by factors to equalize electrons lost/gained

**Step 6:** Complete balancing by inspection

presentation_slides.title: Example: Oxidation Number Method
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 2.1:** Balance: PbS + O2 → PbO + SO2

**Step 1:** PbS + O2 → PbO + SO2

**Step 2:** Pb(+2)S(-2) + O(0) → Pb(+2)O(-2) + S(+4)O2(-2)

**Step 3:**
- S: -2 → +4 (loses 6e-) → Oxidized
- O: 0 → -2 (gains 2e- each) → Reduced

**Step 4:** S loses 6e-, O gains 4e- total

**Step 5:** Multiply O2 by 3/2 to equalize: 6e- lost = 6e- gained

**Step 6:** PbS + 3/2 O2 → PbO + SO2

**Balanced equation:** 2PbS + 3O2 → 2PbO + 2SO2

presentation_slides.title: Half-Reaction Method - Steps
presentation_slides.content:
**Step 1:** Separate into oxidation and reduction half-reactions

**Step 2:** Balance each half-reaction:
- Balance atoms (other than O and H first)
- Balance O: Add H2O
- Balance H: Add H+ (acidic) or H+ + OH- (basic)
- Balance charge: Add e-

**Step 3:** Multiply half-reactions to equalize electrons

**Step 4:** Add half-reactions and cancel electrons

**Step 5:** Check atoms and charges are balanced

presentation_slides.title: Example: Half-Reaction Method (Acidic)
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 2.2:** Balance in acidic medium:
Fe2+ + Cr2O72- → Fe3+ + Cr3+

**Step 1:** Separate half-reactions
- Oxidation: Fe2+ → Fe3+
- Reduction: Cr2O72- → Cr3+

**Step 2:** Balance each
- Oxidation: Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e-
- Reduction (acidic): 14H+ + Cr2O72- + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

**Step 3:** Equalize electrons (multiply oxidation by 6)
- Oxidation: 6Fe2+ → 6Fe3+ + 6e-
- Reduction: 14H+ + Cr2O72- + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

**Step 4:** Add:
6Fe2+ + 14H+ + Cr2O72- → 6Fe3+ + 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

presentation_slides.title: Example: Half-Reaction Method (Basic)
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 2.2:** Balance in basic medium:
MnO4- + I- → MnO2 + I2

**Step 1:** Separate
- Oxidation: I- → I2
- Reduction: MnO4- → MnO2

**Step 2:** Balance (as if acidic first)
- Oxidation: 2I- → I2 + 2e-
- Reduction: MnO4- + 4H+ + 3e- → MnO2 + 2H2O

**Step 3:** Equalize (multiply oxidation by 3, reduction by 2)
- Oxidation: 6I- → 3I2 + 6e-
- Reduction: 2MnO4- + 8H+ + 6e- → 2MnO2 + 4H2O

**Step 4:** Add: 6I- + 2MnO4- + 8H+ → 3I2 + 2MnO2 + 4H2O

**Step 5:** Add OH- to both sides for basic:
6I- + 2MnO4- + 4H2O → 3I2 + 2MnO2 + 8OH-

presentation_slides.title: Section 2.2: Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Differentiate between metallic and electrolytic conductivity
- Draw and label electrolytic cells
- Define preferential discharge
- Explain factors affecting preferential discharge
- Describe electrolysis of dilute H2SO4, NaOH, NaCl
- Describe electrolysis of CuSO4 with inert and active electrodes

presentation_slides.title: Conductivity - Two Types
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Metallic (Electronic) Conduction:**
- Occurs in metals and alloys
- Due to flow of delocalized electrons
- NO chemical change
- Conductivity decreases with temperature

**2. Electrolytic Conduction:**
- Occurs in electrolytes (molten or dissolved)
- Due to movement of ions
- Chemical changes occur at electrodes
- Conductivity increases with temperature

**Key Distinction:**
Metallic conduction = electron flow
Electrolytic conduction = ion movement

presentation_slides.title: Experiment 2.1: Electrical Conductivity Test
presentation_slides.content:
**Objective:** Classify substances as conductors and insulators.

**Materials:**
Copper wire, light bulb, power supply, scotch tape, distilled water, 1M NaCl, 1M H2SO4, 1M CH3COOH, 1M sugar solution, magnesium ribbon, iron nail.

**Procedure:**
1. Polish copper, iron, and magnesium strips
2. Connect as shown in Figure 2.2
3. Test solid materials
4. Test solutions: water, NaCl, H2SO4, CH3COOH, sugar

**Results:**
- **Strong electrolytes:** NaCl, H2SO4 (bright light)
- **Weak electrolyte:** CH3COOH (dim light)
- **Non-electrolyte:** Sugar (no light)
- **Conductors:** Iron, magnesium
- **Insulator:** Sulphur

presentation_slides.title: 2.2.1 Electrolytic Cells
presentation_slides.content:
**What is an Electrolytic Cell?**
A device that uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.

**Components:**
1. **Electrolyte:** Ionic compound in molten or aqueous state
2. **Electrodes:**
   - Anode (+): Oxidation occurs
   - Cathode (-): Reduction occurs
3. **Power Source:** Supplies the electrical energy

**Ion Movement:**
- Cations (+) → move toward cathode (-)
- Anions (-) → move toward anode (+)

**Key Difference from Galvanic Cell:**
- Electrolytic: Non-spontaneous, requires external energy
- Galvanic: Spontaneous, produces electrical energy

presentation_slides.title: 2.2.2 Preferential Discharge
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Preferential discharge is the selective discharge of one type of ion at an electrode when multiple ions are present.

**Factors Affecting Preferential Discharge:**

**1. Position in Electrochemical Series:**
- Ions lower in the series discharge first
- Example: Cu2+ (lower) vs. Na+ (higher) → Cu2+ discharges first

**2. Concentration of Ions:**
- Higher concentration favors discharge
- Example: Concentrated NaCl → Cl- at anode
- Dilute NaCl → OH- at anode

**3. Nature of Electrode:**
- Inert electrodes (graphite, Pt): Don't participate
- Active electrodes (Cu, Ag): Can participate in reaction

presentation_slides.title: Activity Series of Metals
presentation_slides.content:
**Reactivity Series (Table 2.1):**

**Most Reactive (Displace H from cold water, steam, acids):**
Li > K > Ba > Sr > Ca > Na

**Reactive (Displace H from steam and acids):**
Mg > Al > Zn > Cr > Fe > Cd

**Moderately Reactive (Displace H from acids only):**
Co > Ni > Sn > Pb

**Hydrogen:** Included for comparison

**Least Reactive (Unreactive):**
Cu > Hg > Ag > Pt > Au

**Key Rule:**
A metal can displace metal ions BELOW it in the series, but NOT above.

presentation_slides.title: Ease of Discharge of Ions
presentation_slides.content:
**Cations (Discharge at Cathode):**
- From bottom to top (easier to harder):
  Au3+ > Ag+ > Cu2+ > H+ > Fe2+ > Zn2+ > Al3+ > Na+ > K+

**Anions (Discharge at Anode):**
- From bottom to top (easier to harder):
  S2- > I- > Br- > Cl- > OH- > NO3- > SO42-

**Example:**
If a solution has K+ and Cu2+:
- Cu2+ discharges first (lower in series)
- K+ remains in solution

**Example:**
If a solution has OH- and Cl-:
- OH- normally discharges first
- But if Cl- is very concentrated, Cl- may discharge first

presentation_slides.title: 2.2.3 Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions
presentation_slides.content:
**General Process:**
- Ions migrate to electrodes
- Cations reduced at cathode
- Anions oxidized at anode

**Factors to Consider:**
1. Which ions are present?
2. Which ion will discharge preferentially?

**Selected Solutions:**
1. Dilute NaCl
2. Concentrated NaCl (brine)
3. Dilute H2SO4
4. Dilute NaOH
5. CuSO4 (with inert electrodes)
6. CuSO4 (with Cu electrodes)

presentation_slides.title: Electrolysis of Concentrated NaCl (Brine)
presentation_slides.content:
**Ions Present:** Na+, H+, Cl-, OH-

**Cathode (-):**
H+ (reduction potential: -0.83V) vs Na+ (-2.71V)
→ H+ discharges preferentially
2H+ + 2e- → H2(g)

**Anode (+):**
Cl- vs OH- (both possible, but concentrated Cl- wins)
2Cl- → Cl2(g) + 2e-

**Overall Reaction:**
2H+ + 2Cl- → H2(g) + Cl2(g)

**Byproduct:**
NaOH forms as OH- concentration increases

**Uses:**
- H2: Fuel, chemical feedstock
- Cl2: Water treatment, bleach production
- NaOH: Soap, paper, aluminum production

presentation_slides.title: Experiment 2.2: Electrolysis of NaCl
presentation_slides.content:
**Objective:** Electrolyze NaCl solution and observe reactions at electrodes.

**Procedure:**
1. Prepare 0.1 M NaCl solution
2. Transfer to beaker
3. Immerse graphite electrodes
4. Set up as shown in Figure 2.5

**Observations:**
- Gas bubbles at both electrodes
- Cathode: H2 gas (pop test)
- Anode: Cl2 gas (bleach smell)

**Electrode Reactions:**
- Cathode: 2H+ + 2e- → H2(g)
- Anode: 2Cl- → Cl2(g) + 2e-

**Overall:** 2H+ + 2Cl- → H2 + Cl2

presentation_slides.title: Electrolysis of Dilute NaCl
presentation_slides.content:
**Ions Present:** Na+, H+, Cl-, OH-

**At Dilute Concentrations:**
- OH- is lower in electrochemical series than Cl-
- OH- discharges preferentially at anode

**Cathode:**
2H+ + 2e- → H2(g)

**Anode:**
4OH- → 2H2O + O2(g) + 4e-

**Overall Reaction:**
4H+ + 4OH- → 2H2 + O2 + 2H2O
- This is essentially the electrolysis of water!

**Key Difference:**
- Concentrated NaCl → Cl2 at anode
- Dilute NaCl → O2 at anode

presentation_slides.title: Electrolysis of Dilute H2SO4
presentation_slides.content:
**Ions Present:** H+, SO42-, OH-

**Cathode:**
H+ discharges
4H+ + 4e- → 2H2(g)

**Anode:**
OH- discharges (lower than SO42-)
4OH- → 2H2O + O2(g) + 4e-

**Overall Reaction:**
2H2O → 2H2(g) + O2(g)

**Observation:**
- The water decomposes into H2 and O2
- The acid concentration increases (H+ from water left behind)
- Same as electrolysis of water!

presentation_slides.title: Electrolysis of Dilute NaOH
presentation_slides.content:
**Ions Present:** Na+, OH-

**Cathode:**
2H2O + 2e- → H2(g) + 2OH-

**Anode:**
4OH- → 2H2O + O2(g) + 4e-

**Overall Reaction:**
2H2O → 2H2(g) + O2(g)

**Observation:**
- Again, water decomposes!
- Na+ remains in solution
- NaOH concentration increases

**Key Point:**
Electrolysis of dilute H2SO4, NaOH, and NaCl all result in decomposition of water.

presentation_slides.title: Electrolysis of CuSO4 with Inert Electrodes
presentation_slides.content:
**Ions Present:** Cu2+, H+, SO42-, OH-

**Cathode:**
Cu2+ discharges (higher reduction potential than H+)
Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu(s)

**Anode:**
OH- discharges (lower than SO42-)
4OH- → 2H2O + O2(g) + 4e-

**Overall Reaction:**
2Cu2+ + 4OH- → 2Cu(s) + 2H2O + O2(g)

**Results:**
- Cu metal deposited on cathode
- O2 gas evolved at anode
- Solution becomes acidic (H+ and SO42- form H2SO4)

presentation_slides.title: Electrolysis of CuSO4 with Cu Electrodes
presentation_slides.content:
**Active Electrodes (Copper):**

**Cathode:**
Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu(s) (deposited)

**Anode:**
Cu(s) → Cu2+ + 2e- (dissolves)

**Overall Reaction:**
Cu(anode) → Cu(cathode)

**Results:**
- Mass of cathode increases
- Mass of anode decreases
- CuSO4 concentration remains constant
- This is the principle of **copper refining**

**Application:**
- Purification of copper
- Electroplating of copper

presentation_slides.title: Section 2.3: Quantitative Aspects of Electrolysis
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- State Faraday's first law of electrolysis
- Write mathematical expressions for the first law
- Perform calculations using the first law
- State Faraday's second law of electrolysis
- Write mathematical expressions for the second law
- Perform calculations using the second law

presentation_slides.title: 2.3.1 Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis
presentation_slides.content:
**Statement:**
The mass of a substance (m) deposited or dissolved at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity (Q) passed through the electrolyte.

**Mathematically:**
- m ∝ Q
- m = zQ (where z is electrochemical equivalent)
- m = (E × I × t) / F

**Where:**
- E = Equivalent weight of substance
- I = Current in amperes
- t = Time in seconds
- F = Faraday's Constant = 96,500 C/mol e-

**Equivalent Weight:**
E = Molar mass / Valence

**Alternative Form:**
m = (M × I × t) / (n × F)
Where n = number of electrons transferred per ion

presentation_slides.title: Understanding the First Law
presentation_slides.content:
**Key Relationships:**

1 mole of electrons = 6.02 × 1023 electrons = 96,500 C (1 Faraday)

**Examples:**
- To deposit 1 mol of Na: need 1 mol e-
- To deposit 1 mol of Mg: need 2 mol e-
- To deposit 1 mol of Al: need 3 mol e-

**Half-Reactions:**
- Na+ + e- → Na
- Mg2+ + 2e- → Mg
- Al3+ + 3e- → Al

**Stoichiometry:**
- 2 mol e- produce 1 mol Mg (24.3 g)
- 3 mol e- produce 1 mol Al (27.0 g)
- 1 mol e- produces 1 mol Ag (107.9 g)

presentation_slides.title: Example: Faraday's First Law Calculation
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 2.4:**
Calculate the mass of calcium metal and chlorine gas produced when a current of 0.452 A is passed through molten CaCl2 for 1.5 h.

**Step 1:** Write half-reactions
- Cathode: Ca2+ + 2e- → Ca(s)
- Anode: 2Cl- → Cl2(g) + 2e-

**Step 2:** Calculate charge
Q = I × t = 0.452 A × (1.5 × 60 × 60 s) = 0.452 × 5400 = 2440.8 C

**Step 3:** Calculate moles of electrons
moles e- = Q / F = 2440.8 / 96,500 = 0.0253 mol e-

**Step 4:** Calculate mass of Ca
2 mol e- → 1 mol Ca (40.08 g)
0.0253 mol e- → x g Ca
x = (0.0253 × 40.08) / 2 = 0.507 g Ca

**Step 5:** Calculate mass of Cl2
2 mol e- → 1 mol Cl2 (71 g)
0.0253 mol e- → x g Cl2
x = (0.0253 × 71) / 2 = 0.898 g Cl2

presentation_slides.title: 2.3.2 Faraday's Second Law of Electrolysis
presentation_slides.content:
**Statement:**
The masses of different substances liberated or dissolved by the same quantity of electricity are proportional to their equivalent masses.

**Mathematically:**
m1 / m2 = E1 / E2

**For Multiple Cells in Series:**
m1 / E1 = m2 / E2 = m3 / E3 = k (constant)

**Example:**
Three cells connected in series with H2SO4, CuSO4, and AgNO3:
- H2SO4: H2 and O2 liberated
- CuSO4: Cu deposited
- AgNO3: Ag deposited

presentation_slides.title: Example: Faraday's Second Law Calculation
presentation_slides.content:
**Example 2.5:**
Calculate the mass of copper deposited by electrolysis of CuSO4 in series with AgNO3 when 0.108 g of Ag is deposited.

**Step 1:** Find equivalent weights
- Ag: Ag+ + e- → Ag
  EAg = 108 / 1 = 108 g/eq
- Cu: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu
  ECu = 63.5 / 2 = 31.75 g/eq

**Step 2:** Use the proportion
mAg / EAg = mCu / ECu

**Step 3:** Solve for mCu
mCu = (ECu × mAg) / EAg
mCu = (31.75 × 0.108) / 108
mCu = 0.032 g

presentation_slides.title: Section 2.4: Industrial Applications of Electrolysis
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Mention industrial applications of electrolysis
- Explain electroplating and electrorefining
- Demonstrate copper refining
- Explain how electrolysis is used to produce metals, nonmetals, and compounds

presentation_slides.title: Industrial Applications of Electrolysis
presentation_slides.content:
**Major Applications:**

1. **Extraction of Highly Reactive Metals**
   - Aluminum, sodium, magnesium
   - Can't be obtained by chemical reduction

2. **Refining of Metals**
   - Purification of copper, zinc, tin
   - Removes impurities

3. **Electroplating**
   - Decorative coating
   - Corrosion protection

4. **Production of Nonmetals and Compounds**
   - Chlorine, sodium hydroxide
   - Fluorine

presentation_slides.title: Extraction of Metals by Electrolysis
presentation_slides.content:
**Why Electrolysis for Active Metals?**
Metals more reactive than carbon cannot be reduced by carbon.

**Example: Extraction of Aluminum**

**Raw Material:** Bauxite (Al2O3)

**Process:**
- Electrolyte: Molten Al2O3 in cryolite
- Electrodes: Graphite

**Reactions:**
- Cathode (reduction): 4Al3+ + 12e- → 4Al
- Anode (oxidation): 6O2- → 3O2 + 12e-
- Overall: 4Al3+ + 6O2- → 4Al + 3O2

**Products:**
- Molten aluminum at cathode (drains away)
- Oxygen gas at anode (bubbles off)

presentation_slides.title: Electrolytic Refining of Copper
presentation_slides.content:
**Figure 2.7: Purification of Copper by Electrolysis**

**Setup:**
- Anode: Impure copper
- Cathode: Pure copper strip
- Electrolyte: CuSO4 solution with acid

**Reactions:**
- Anode: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e- (copper dissolves)
- Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (pure copper deposits)

**Impurities:**
- Soluble impurities: Go into solution
- Insoluble impurities: Settle as "anode mud"

**Anode Mud Contains:**
- Gold, silver, platinum, other precious metals
- Can be recovered separately

presentation_slides.title: Experiment 2.3: Electroplating an Iron Key with Copper
presentation_slides.content:
**Objective:** Electroplate an iron key with copper.

**Setup (Figure 2.8):**
- Anode (+): Copper plate
- Cathode (-): Iron key
- Electrolyte: CuSO4 + H2SO4

**Procedure:**
1. Clean copper plate and iron key with sandpaper
2. Place copper plate as anode (positive terminal)
3. Place iron key as cathode (negative terminal)
4. Pass current for 15 minutes
5. Remove and observe

**Observations:**
- Iron key becomes coated with copper
- Copper plate loses mass

**Reactions:**
- Anode: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-
- Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu

presentation_slides.title: Section 2.5: Voltaic Cells
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn:
- Define voltaic cells and salt bridges
- Define electrode potential and cell potential
- Explain standard electrode potential measurement
- Describe the electrochemical series
- Use the Nernst equation
- Understand concentration cells
- Explain corrosion and its prevention

presentation_slides.title: Introduction to Voltaic Cells
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
A voltaic (galvanic) cell converts chemical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.

**Key Differences from Electrolytic Cell:**
| Feature | Voltaic Cell | Electrolytic Cell |
|---------|--------------|-------------------|
| Reaction | Spontaneous | Non-spontaneous |
| Energy | Produces electrical energy | Consumes electrical energy |
| Anode | Negative (-) | Positive (+) |
| Cathode | Positive (+) | Negative (-) |

**Example: Daniell Cell**
- Zn/ZnSO4 half-cell
- Cu/CuSO4 half-cell

presentation_slides.title: The Daniell Cell - Construction
presentation_slides.content:
**Figure 2.9: Daniell Cell**

**Components:**
1. Zn electrode in ZnSO4 solution (anode)
2. Cu electrode in CuSO4 solution (cathode)
3. Salt bridge connecting solutions
4. External wire connecting electrodes

**Reactions:**
- Anode (oxidation): Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-
- Cathode (reduction): Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu
- Overall: Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu

**Electron Flow:**
Zn → wire → Cu (external circuit)

**Ion Flow:**
- K+ from salt bridge → CuSO4 solution
- Cl- from salt bridge → ZnSO4 solution

presentation_slides.title: Purpose of the Salt Bridge
presentation_slides.content:
**Function:**
- Completes the electrical circuit
- Maintains charge neutrality

**Problem without Salt Bridge:**
- As Zn dissolves: [Zn2+] increases → positive charge builds up
- As Cu deposits: [Cu2+] decreases → negative charge builds up
- This charge buildup stops the reaction

**How Salt Bridge Works:**
- Ions move to balance charge
- K+ moves to cathode (CuSO4) to balance negative charge
- Cl- moves to anode (ZnSO4) to balance positive charge

**Ideal Salt Bridge Electrolyte:**
- Ions that won't react with other ions or electrodes
- Common choices: KCl, KNO3, NH4NO3

presentation_slides.title: Cell Notation
presentation_slides.content:
**Purpose:** Shorthand notation for voltaic cells.

**Conventions:**
- Anode (oxidation) on LEFT
- Cathode (reduction) on RIGHT
- Single line | = phase boundary (electrode | solution)
- Double line || = salt bridge

**Example: Daniell Cell**
Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s)

**With Concentrations:**
Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq, 1.0M) || Cu2+(aq, 1.0M) | Cu(s)

**General Form:**
anode | anode electrolyte || cathode electrolyte | cathode

**For Inert Electrodes (graphite):**
graphite | I-(aq) | I2(s) || MnO4-(aq), H+(aq), Mn2+(aq) | graphite

presentation_slides.title: Standard Electrode Potentials
presentation_slides.content:
**The Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE):**

**Reference Electrode:**
2H+(1M) + 2e- → H2(1 atm) E° = 0.00 V

**Construction (Figure 2.10):**
- Pt electrode
- H2 gas at 1 atm
- HCl solution at 1 M

**Measuring Unknown Potentials:**
E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode

**Example - Zn/Zn2+:**
- Zn electrode with SHE
- E°cell = 0.76 V
- E°cell = E°H+/H2 - E°Zn2+/Zn
- 0.76 = 0 - E°Zn2+/Zn
- E°Zn2+/Zn = -0.76 V

presentation_slides.title: Standard Reduction Potentials Table
presentation_slides.content:
**Table 2.3: Standard Reduction Potentials (25°C)**

| Half-Reaction | E° (V) |
|---------------|--------|
| F2 + 2e- → 2F- | +2.87 |
| Au3+ + 3e- → Au | +1.50 |
| Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl- | +1.36 |
| O2 + 4H+ + 4e- → 2H2O | +1.23 |
| Ag+ + e- → Ag | +0.80 |
| Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu | +0.34 |
| 2H+ + 2e- → H2 | 0.00 |
| Fe2+ + 2e- → Fe | -0.44 |
| Zn2+ + 2e- → Zn | -0.76 |
| Al3+ + 3e- → Al | -1.66 |
| Mg2+ + 2e- → Mg | -2.37 |
| Na+ + e- → Na | -2.71 |
| Li+ + e- → Li | -3.05 |

**Key Relationships:**
- Higher E° = stronger oxidizing agent (left side)
- Lower (more negative) E° = stronger reducing agent (right side)

presentation_slides.title: Calculating Cell Potential
presentation_slides.content:
**Formula:**
E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode

**Example 2.7:**
Calculate E°cell for a cell with Mg and Ag electrodes.

**Step 1:** Identify half-reactions
- Mg2+ + 2e- → Mg: E° = -2.37 V
- Ag+ + e- → Ag: E° = +0.80 V

**Step 2:** Determine anode and cathode
- Ag will be reduced (higher E°): cathode
- Mg will be oxidized (lower E°): anode

**Step 3:** Calculate
E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode
E°cell = 0.80 - (-2.37) = 3.17 V

**Interpretation:**
Positive E°cell = spontaneous reaction

presentation_slides.title: The Nernst Equation
presentation_slides.content:
**Purpose:** Calculate cell potential under non-standard conditions.

**Equation:**
Ecell = E°cell - (0.0592/n) log Q

**Where:**
- Ecell = cell potential (non-standard)
- E°cell = standard cell potential
- n = number of electrons transferred
- Q = reaction quotient

**Example:**
For Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu
E°cell = 1.10 V, n = 2

If [Cu2+] = 0.100 M and [Zn2+] = 1.0 × 10-5 M:
Q = [Zn2+] / [Cu2+] = (1.0 × 10-5) / 0.100 = 1.0 × 10-4
Ecell = 1.10 - (0.0592/2) log(1.0 × 10-4)
Ecell = 1.10 - (0.0296)(-4) = 1.10 + 0.118 = 1.22 V

presentation_slides.title: Concentration Cells
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
A voltaic cell with two half-cells of the same material but different concentrations.

**Figure 2.14: Concentration Cell**

**Example:** Cu | Cu2+(0.10M) || Cu2+(1.0M) | Cu

**Reactions:**
- Anode (dilute): Cu → Cu2+(0.10M) + 2e-
- Cathode (concentrated): Cu2+(1.0M) + 2e- → Cu

**Overall:** Cu2+(1.0M) → Cu2+(0.10M)

**Cell Potential:**
Ecell = 0 - (0.0592/2) log(0.10/1.0) = 0 + 0.0296 = 0.0296 V

**How It Works:**
- Dilute solution becomes more concentrated
- Concentrated solution becomes more dilute
- Cell operates until concentrations are equal

presentation_slides.title: Batteries - Types
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Primary Batteries (Non-rechargeable):**
- Chemical reaction is irreversible
- Discarded when dead

**Examples:**
- Dry cell (Leclanché cell)
- Alkaline battery
- Mercury battery

**2. Secondary Batteries (Rechargeable):**
- Chemical reaction is reversible
- Can be recharged

**Examples:**
- Lead-storage battery (car battery)
- Nickel-cadmium battery
- Lithium-ion battery

**3. Fuel Cells:**
- Require continuous supply of reactants
- Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell (Figure 2.16)

presentation_slides.title: Corrosion - The Rusting of Iron
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Corrosion is the deterioration of metals by an electrochemical process.

**Key Facts about Rusting:**
1. Moisture must be present
2. Oxygen must be present
3. Occurs at different places on the same object
4. Faster at low pH
5. Faster in ionic solutions

**Electrochemical Process:**
- Anodic region (site of iron loss):
  Fe → Fe2+ + 2e-
- Cathodic region (site of oxygen reduction):
  O2 + 4H+ + 4e- → 2H2O

presentation_slides.title: Corrosion Prevention Methods
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Protective Coating:**
- Paint, oil, grease
- Problem: Damage exposes bare metal

**2. Galvanizing (Sacrificial Protection):**
- Coat iron with zinc
- Zinc is more active (E° = -0.76 V vs -0.44 V for Fe)
- Zinc corrodes instead of iron
- "Sacrificial anode"

**3. Cathodic Protection:**
- Connect iron to a more active metal
- Example: Mg or Zn attached to pipelines, ships
- Active metal acts as anode
- Iron becomes cathode (protected)

**4. Alloying:**
- Stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni)
- Chromium oxide layer protects

**5. Barrier Methods:**
- Non-conducting rubber/plastic spacers
- Prevents metal-metal contact

presentation_slides.title: Figure 2.18 & 2.19: Metal-Metal Contact
presentation_slides.content:
**Figure 2.18: Fe in contact with Cu (corrodes faster)**

- Cu is less active than Fe
- Fe acts as anode (loses electrons)
- Corrosion is enhanced

**Why?**
- Fe prefers to be oxidized vs Cu
- Creates a galvanic couple

**Figure 2.19: Fe in contact with Zn (no corrosion)**

- Zn is more active than Fe
- Zn acts as anode (sacrificial)
- Fe acts as cathode (protected)

**This is "Cathodic Protection"**

**Application:**
- Galvanized steel
- Sacrificial anodes on ships
- Underground pipelines

presentation_slides.title: What is Industrial Chemistry?
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
A branch of chemistry that applies physical and chemical procedures to transform natural raw materials and their derivatives into products beneficial to humanity.

**Key Role:**
Bridges the gap between chemistry as taught in schools and chemistry as practiced commercially.

**Historical Context:**
- 19th century industrial revolution

- Demand for chemical products increased

presentation_slides.title: Characteristics of Chemical Industries
presentation_slides.content:

1. **Raw Materials:**

2. **Chemical Reactions:**

3. **Energy Consumption:**

4. **Safety:**

5. **Quality Control:**

   - Ensure products meet specifications

presentation_slides.title: Section 3.2: Natural Resources and Industry

presentation_slides.title: 3.2.1 Natural Resources - Sources
presentation_slides.content:
**Natural Resources are Raw Materials from:**

**1. Atmosphere:**

**3. Lithosphere:**

presentation_slides.title: Classification of Natural Resources
presentation_slides.content:
**1. Renewable Resources:**

**Definition:** Can be replenished through rapid natural cycles.

- Leather, pulp products

**2. Non-Renewable Resources:**

**Definition:** Exist in fixed amounts, cannot be replenished.

**Examples:**

presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn about:

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.1 Ammonia - Haber-Bosch Process
presentation_slides.content:
**Properties of Ammonia:**
- Colorless gas, sharp irritating odor
- Density: 0.769 kg/m3 (lighter than air)
- Melting point: -77.7°C, Boiling point: -33.35°C
- Highly soluble in water (34% w/w at 25°C)
- Weak base (forms NH4OH in water)

**Uses of Ammonia:**
- Cleaning agent, antimicrobial agent
- Raw material for nitrogen fertilizers
- Explosives (nitrocellulose, TNT)
- Soda ash production
- Nitric acid production (Ostwald process)

presentation_slides.title: The Haber-Bosch Process
presentation_slides.content:
**Reaction:**
N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (ΔH = -92 kJ/mol)

**Conditions:**
- Temperature: 300-500°C
- Pressure: 15-25 MPa
- Catalyst: Finely divided iron

**Source of Reactants:**
- N2: Fractional distillation of air
- H2: Natural gas (methane) reforming

**Process Steps:**
1. Prepare H2 and N2
2. React in chamber with iron catalyst
3. Condense NH3 (boils at -33°C)
4. Recycle unreacted gases

**Yield:** ~97% conversion

presentation_slides.title: Figure 3.2: Ammonia Production
presentation_slides.content:
[Figure 3.2: Production of NH3 using Haber-Bosch process]

**Key Features:**
1. Hydrogen and nitrogen mixed
2. Passed over iron catalyst
3. High pressure and moderate temperature
4. Ammonia condensed out
5. Unreacted gases recycled

**Le Chatelier's Principle:**
- High pressure favors product (fewer gas moles)
- Low temperature favors product (exothermic)
- But low temperature slows reaction
- Catalyst allows moderate temperature

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.2 Nitric Acid - Ostwald Process
presentation_slides.content:
**Properties:**
- Colorless liquid, pungent odor
- Density: 1.51 g/cm3
- Turns brown on exposure to light (forms NO2)
- Strong acid, strong oxidizing agent
- Highly corrosive

**Uses:**
- Ammonium nitrate fertilizer
- Organic nitrogen compounds (nitrobenzene)
- Explosives (TNT, nitroglycerine)
- Plastics, drugs, dyes

**Reaction with Light:**
4HNO3 → 4NO2 + O2 + 2H2O (brown gas)

presentation_slides.title: The Ostwald Process - Steps
presentation_slides.content:
**Step 1:** Oxidation of ammonia
4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O
Catalyst: Pt, Temperature: 850°C

**Step 2:** Oxidation of NO to NO2
2NO + O2 → 2NO2

**Step 3:** Absorption in water
3NO2 + H2O → 2HNO3 + NO

**Recycling:**
- NO from Step 3 returned to Step 2
- Maximizes efficiency

**Figure 3.7:** Nitric acid manufacturing process flow

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.3 Nitrogen-Based Fertilizers
presentation_slides.content:
**Types of Nitrogen Fertilizers:**

1. **Anhydrous Ammonia (NH3):**
   - Pressurized liquid
   - Injected into soil
   - Most basic form

2. **Urea ((NH2)2CO):**
   - 46% nitrogen content
   - Reacts: 2NH3 + CO2 → (NH2)2CO + H2O
   - Soil reaction: (NH2)2CO + H2O → CO2 + 2NH3

3. **UAN Solutions:**
   - Urea + ammonium nitrate in water
   - 50% amide-N, 25% ammonium-N, 25% nitrate-N

4. **DAP ((NH4)2HPO4):**
   - Contains N and P
   - Produced from NH3 + H3PO4

presentation_slides.title: DAP - Diammonium Monohydrogen Phosphate
presentation_slides.content:
**Production:**

**Step 1:**
3NH3 + 2H3PO4 → NH4H2PO4 + (NH4)2HPO4

**Step 2:**
NH4H2PO4 + NH3 → (NH4)2HPO4

**Uses of DAP:**
- Fertilizer (both N and P essential)
- Fire retardant
- Yeast nutrient in wine and beer making

**Soil Reaction:**
- Temporarily increases soil acidity
- Long-term: becomes more acidic
- Nitrification of ammonium contributes to acidification

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.4 Sulfuric Acid - Contact Process
presentation_slides.content:
**Properties:**
- Colorless, odorless, heavy oily liquid
- Molar mass: 98 g/mol
- Melting point: 10.5°C, Boiling point: 338°C
- Highly corrosive, exothermic with water
- Strong oxidizing and dehydrating agent

**Common Concentrations:**
- 33.5%: Battery acid
- 62.18%: Chamber acid (fertilizer production)

**Reaction with Metals:**
Cu + 2H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O

presentation_slides.title: The Contact Process - Steps
presentation_slides.content:
**Step 1: Production of SO2**
S + O2 → SO2 (burning sulfur)
Or: 4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2 (roasting pyrite)

**Step 2: Oxidation of SO2 to SO3**
2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3
Catalyst: V2O5, Temperature: 400-450°C, Pressure: 1-2 atm

**Step 3: Formation of Oleum**
SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7 (oleum)

**Step 4: Dilution to Sulfuric Acid**
H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4

**Figure 3.10:** Production of sulfuric acid (contact process)

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.5 Pesticides and Herbicides
presentation_slides.content:
**Definition:**
Chemicals used to prevent or control pests, diseases, weeds, and other plant pathogens.

**Classification of Pesticides:**

1. **Organochlorines:**
   - C, H, Cl, O atoms
   - Soluble in lipids, accumulate in fatty tissue
   - Toxic to many animals, long-term persistence

2. **Organophosphates:**
   - Phosphorus-containing
   - Less persistent than organochlorines

3. **Carbamates:**
   - Derived from carbamic acid
   - Shorter persistence

**Herbicides:**
- Chlorophenoxy acids (2,4-D, 2,4,5-T)
- Triazines (atrazine, simazine, hexazinone)

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.6 Sodium Carbonate - Solvay Process
presentation_slides.content:
**Properties:**
- White crystalline solid
- Na2CO3·10H2O (decahydrate)
- Melting point: 851°C, Boiling point: 1600°C
- Hygroscopic, soluble in water
- Forms alkaline solution (hydrolysis)

**Uses:**
- Glass manufacturing
- Detergents, soaps
- Water softening
- Paper production

**Solvay Process (Figure 3.10):**
- Raw materials: NaCl, CaCO3, NH3, H2O
- Main reactions given in textbook

presentation_slides.title: 3.3.7 Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH)
presentation_slides.content:
**Properties:**
- White, translucent crystalline solid
- Melting point: 591 K
- Corrosive (caustic soda)
- Dissolves readily in water (alkaline solution)
- Moderately soluble in alcohol

**Production Methods:**
1. Castner-Kellner process (mercury cathode)
2. Nelson Diaphragm cell
3. Loewig's process

**Castner-Kellner Process:**
- Brine solution (NaCl)
- Anode: Titanium (Cl2 produced)
- Cathode: Mercury (Na amalgam formed)
- Na amalgam + H2O → NaOH + H2 + Hg

presentation_slides.title: NaOH - Reactions and Uses
presentation_slides.content:
**Reactions:**
Anode: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-
Cathode: 2Na+ + 2e- → 2Na (amalgam)
Amalgam: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2

**Uses:**
- Pulp and paper manufacturing
- Alumina extraction from bauxite (aluminum)
- Textiles industry
- Drinking water production
- Soap and detergents
- Washing soda production
- Saponification reactions
- Basic catalyst

**Safety:**
- Corrosive (skin and eye irritation)
- High affinity for water (forms hydrates)
- Requires careful storage

presentation_slides.title: Section 3.4: Manufacturing Industries in Ethiopia
presentation_slides.content:
In this section, we will learn about:
- Glass manufacturing
- Ceramics manufacturing

- Sugar manufacturing
